questions.explain: 지문은 당시 여성이 연구선에 오르는 것이 종종 금지되어 그녀가 육상에서 일했다고 밝힌다.

questions.q: The word 'conjecture' as used in the passage most nearly means
options: proven fact
unsupported guess
official map
careful measurement
questions.explain: 동료가 그녀의 생각을 너무 급진적이라며 'mere conjecture'라 일축한 맥락에서 '근거 없는 추측'이 가장 가깝다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about Tharp's character from the passage?
options: She gave up easily under criticism
She was persistent and trusted her careful evidence
She had no interest in accuracy
She avoided difficult problems
questions.explain: 동료의 일축에도 증거를 계속 다듬어 패턴을 입증했다는 서술에서 끈기 있고 자기 작업을 신뢰하는 성격을 추론할 수 있다.

title: How Lichens Survive
passage: A lichen is not a single organism but a partnership. It forms when a fungus and an alga, and sometimes a cyanobacterium, live together so closely that they behave as one body. The fungus builds a protective structure and gathers moisture and minerals, while the alga uses sunlight to make sugars that feed the whole arrangement. Because each partner supplies what the other lacks, lichens can colonize bare rock, frozen tundra, and desert crusts where few plants take hold. They grow slowly, often less than a millimeter a year, yet some patches are estimated to be thousands of years old. This durability has a cost: lichens absorb water and gases directly through their surfaces, with no roots or protective skin to filter what enters. As a result, they readily take up pollutants from the air. Scientists exploit this sensitivity by surveying lichen communities near cities and factories. Where certain species thin out or vanish, the data point to rising levels of sulfur dioxide or heavy metals, making these quiet organisms reliable, inexpensive monitors of environmental health.

questions.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Lichens are fungi that have evolved the ability to photosynthesize on their own.
Lichens are partnerships whose unusual biology makes them both hardy and useful as pollution indicators.
Lichens grow so slowly that they are of little interest to scientists.
Lichens compete with plants for space on rocks and in deserts.
questions.explain: 지문은 지의류가 균류와 조류의 '동반자 관계'이며, 그 생물학적 특성 덕분에 강인하면서도 오염 지표로 유용하다고 전체적으로 설명한다.

questions.q: According to the passage, why are lichens able to take up pollutants so easily?
options: They have deep roots that draw chemicals from the soil.
They absorb water and gases directly through their surfaces without a protective skin.
They actively seek out polluted areas to feed.
They store sulfur dioxide to use as a nutrient.
questions.explain: 지문은 지의류가 뿌리나 보호 피부 없이 표면을 통해 물과 기체를 직접 흡수하기 때문에 오염물질도 쉽게 흡수한다고 명시한다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about an area where pollution-sensitive lichen species have disappeared?
options: The area likely has poor air quality with elevated pollutants.
The area must be a frozen tundra.
The area has unusually clean air.
The lichens were eaten by animals.
questions.explain: 지문에 따르면 특정 종이 줄거나 사라지면 이산화황이나 중금속 농도 상승을 가리키므로, 그 지역의 대기 질이 나쁠 가능성이 높다고 추론할 수 있다.

title: The Pony Express
passage: In April 1860, a private company launched the Pony Express, a relay of horseback riders carrying mail across nearly two thousand miles between Missouri and California. Before this service, a letter could take weeks to cross the continent by stagecoach or ship. The Express promised delivery in about ten days. To achieve such speed, the company built a chain of stations roughly ten miles apart, where a rider could swap an exhausted horse for a fresh one in under two minutes. Riders were chosen for being light and fearless; advertisements reportedly favored young, wiry men willing to risk danger. Yet the venture was brief. It operated for only eighteen months, and its owners lost money the entire time, largely because the cost of horses, stations, and wages far exceeded the postage collected. What finally ended it was technology. In October 1861, crews completed the transcontinental telegraph, allowing messages to cross the country in minutes rather than days. The Pony Express closed almost immediately, remembered less for profit than for the daring image it left behind.

questions.q: What was the primary reason the Pony Express stopped operating?
options: Riders refused to continue the dangerous work.
The completion of the transcontinental telegraph made it obsolete.
The stations were destroyed in a storm.
California no longer wanted mail from the East.
questions.explain: 지문은 1861년 대륙횡단 전신이 완성되어 메시지가 며칠이 아닌 몇 분 만에 전달되자 포니 익스프레스가 거의 즉시 문을 닫았다고 밝힌다.

questions.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The Pony Express was financially successful throughout its operation.
The Pony Express is remembered more for its bold image than for being a profitable business.
Stagecoaches were faster than the Pony Express.
The telegraph took longer than ten days to deliver messages.
questions.explain: 지문은 회사가 운영 내내 손해를 봤으며 이익보다 대담한 이미지로 기억된다고 서술하므로, 수익보다 이미지로 기억된다는 결론이 가장 타당하다.

questions.q: How long did the Pony Express operate?
options: About ten days
About eighteen months
About ten years
About two thousand days
questions.explain: 지문은 이 서비스가 단 18개월간 운영되었다고 명시한다.

questions.q: As used in the passage, the word 'wiry' most nearly means
options: wealthy and well-connected
lean and physically tough
tall and heavy
experienced and elderly
questions.explain: 지문은 가볍고 두려움 없는 라이더를 선호했다고 했고 'young, wiry men'이라 했으므로 'wiry'는 마르고 단단한, 다부진을 뜻한다.

title: Radar Over Britain
passage: In the late 1930s, British scientists raced to perfect a defensive system that would soon prove decisive. Known then as Radio Direction Finding, it used radio waves bounced off distant aircraft to reveal their range and bearing long before they could be seen or heard. The military built a coastal chain of tall transmitter towers, each sweeping the sky and feeding readings to central rooms where operators plotted incoming formations on large maps. The value of the system lay not only in detection but in coordination. Commanders could now direct a limited number of fighter squadrons to exactly where they were needed, instead of wasting them on constant patrols. During the Battle of Britain in 1940, this advantage helped a smaller defending force meet wave after wave of attacking bombers with surprising efficiency. Crucially, the radar stations were linked by telephone to observers, plotters, and airfields, forming an early integrated network. Historians often note that the technology mattered less in isolation than as part of this command system, which turned scattered warnings into swift, organized action.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest was the most important contribution of the radar system?
options: It allowed Britain to build more bombers than its enemies.
It enabled early detection combined with coordinated direction of limited fighter forces.
It replaced the need for any human operators.
It made coastal towers unnecessary.
questions.explain: 지문은 이 시스템의 가치가 탐지뿐 아니라 제한된 전투기 부대를 필요한 곳으로 조율하는 데 있었다고 강조한다.

questions.q: Why does the passage emphasize the telephone links between stations, observers, and airfields?
options: To show that the radar towers were poorly built.
To illustrate that the technology worked best as part of an integrated command network.
To argue that telephones were more important than radar.
To explain why patrols increased during the battle.
questions.explain: 지문은 기술이 단독보다 명령 체계의 일부로서 흩어진 경보를 신속하고 조직적인 행동으로 바꿨다는 점을 강조하기 위해 전화 연결을 언급한다.

questions.q: Before radar, how were fighter squadrons reportedly used, according to the passage?
options: They were directed precisely to incoming aircraft.
They were wasted on constant patrols.
They were kept entirely on the ground.
They were sent only at night.
questions.explain: 지문은 레이더 덕분에 지휘관들이 끊임없는 순찰로 전투기를 낭비하는 대신 정확히 필요한 곳으로 보낼 수 있었다고 서술한다.

title: Why Passwords Persist
passage: Despite decades of warnings about their weaknesses, passwords remain the most common way people prove their identity online. Security experts have long criticized them: users pick predictable words, reuse the same secret across many sites, and fall prey to scams that trick them into typing credentials into fake pages. Newer methods promise improvement. Hardware keys, fingerprint scanners, and one-time codes sent to phones all reduce certain risks. Yet none has fully displaced the humble password, and the reasons are as much social as technical. Passwords cost nothing to issue, work on nearly any device, and require no special equipment. A small website can adopt them instantly, whereas distributing physical keys to millions of users is expensive and slow. Familiarity also matters; people understand passwords, even badly chosen ones, far better than newer schemes. Many organizations therefore layer extra checks on top of passwords rather than abandoning them. The likely future is not the sudden death of the password but its gradual demotion, surviving as one factor among several rather than the lone gatekeeper it has long been.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: Passwords have already been replaced by fingerprint scanners.
Passwords endure because of practical advantages and will likely become one factor among several rather than disappear.
Passwords are perfectly secure and need no improvement.
Hardware keys are too dangerous for ordinary users.
questions.explain: 지문은 비밀번호가 실용적 이점 때문에 살아남았고, 사라지기보다 여러 요소 중 하나로 점차 강등될 것이라고 결론짓는다.

questions.q: According to the passage, why have alternatives like hardware keys not fully replaced passwords?
options: They are illegal in most countries.
Distributing them is expensive and slow, and passwords are free and familiar.
They offer no security improvement at all.
They work only on a single brand of phone.
questions.explain: 지문은 수백만 사용자에게 물리적 키를 배포하는 것이 비싸고 느린 반면 비밀번호는 무료이고 익숙하다고 설명한다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about how many organizations currently handle password weaknesses?
options: They eliminate passwords entirely.
They add extra verification steps on top of passwords.
They forbid the use of phones for codes.
They ignore the problem completely.
questions.explain: 지문은 많은 조직이 비밀번호를 버리기보다 그 위에 추가 확인 절차를 덧붙인다고 명시하므로 이를 추론할 수 있다.

title: The Bystander Effect
passage: When someone collapses on a crowded street, common sense suggests that more onlookers mean a better chance of help. Research in social psychology often finds the opposite. In a series of experiments, individuals were placed in situations that seemed to require assistance, sometimes alone and sometimes surrounded by others. People who believed they were the only witness tended to act quickly. Those who thought several others were present were slower to respond, and many did nothing at all. Two explanations are usually offered. The first is a diffusion of responsibility: when many could help, each person feels less personally obligated, assuming someone else will step in. The second is social influence; people look to the reactions of those around them to judge whether a situation is truly an emergency, and if everyone appears calm, each concludes there is no need to act. Understanding these patterns has practical value. Safety trainers now advise victims to address one specific person directly, pointing and giving a clear instruction. Naming an individual cuts through the crowd's shared hesitation and assigns responsibility that no one can quietly pass along.

questions.q: What is the main point the passage makes about crowds and helping behavior?
options: Larger crowds always provide faster help.
The presence of many onlookers can actually reduce the speed and likelihood of help.
People never help strangers in any situation.
Emergencies rarely occur in public places.
questions.explain: 지문은 많은 방관자의 존재가 오히려 도움의 속도와 가능성을 낮출 수 있다고 핵심적으로 주장한다.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is 'diffusion of responsibility'?
options: The belief that an emergency is fake.
The feeling that one is less personally obligated to help when others could also act.
The tendency to help only close friends.
The spreading of news about an accident.
questions.explain: 지문은 책임 분산을 '많은 사람이 도울 수 있을 때 각자가 개인적 의무를 덜 느끼는 것'으로 정의한다.

questions.q: Why do safety trainers advise victims to point at one specific person?
options: Because that person is usually a trained doctor.
Because naming an individual assigns responsibility that cannot be passed to others.
Because crowds dislike being addressed.
Because it frightens the rest of the onlookers away.
questions.explain: 지문은 특정 개인을 지목하면 누구도 조용히 떠넘길 수 없는 책임을 부여해 군중의 망설임을 끊는다고 설명한다.

title: The Cost of Free Shipping
passage: Many online shoppers have come to expect delivery at no charge, and retailers compete to offer it. Yet shipping is never truly free; someone pays for the trucks, fuel, and labor that move a package from warehouse to doorstep. The question is how those costs are hidden. Some sellers fold the expense into the product price, quietly raising the listed amount so the bottom line covers delivery. Others set a minimum order, encouraging customers to add items they had not planned to buy in order to qualify. A third approach ties free shipping to membership programs, where an annual fee spread across many orders makes each delivery feel costless even though it is not. Economists note that these tactics work partly because of how people perceive prices. A single visible shipping charge feels like a penalty and can drive shoppers to abandon their carts, while the same money buried in a higher price provokes little resistance. The lesson is not that free shipping is a trick, but that convenience has a price, even when that price is carefully arranged to stay out of sight.

questions.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Free shipping always loses money for retailers.
Shipping costs are real but are hidden in various ways that shape how shoppers perceive prices.
Online shopping is cheaper than visiting physical stores.
Membership programs are the only honest way to charge for delivery.
questions.explain: 지문은 배송비가 실재하지만 여러 방식으로 숨겨지며, 그것이 소비자의 가격 인식에 영향을 준다는 점을 중심 내용으로 다룬다.

questions.q: According to the passage, why might a separate shipping charge cause shoppers to abandon their carts?
options: Because it is always larger than the product price.
Because a visible charge feels like a penalty, while the same cost hidden in a higher price provokes little resistance.
Because shipping charges are illegal in some places.
Because shoppers cannot afford any delivery at all.
questions.explain: 지문은 눈에 보이는 배송비는 벌금처럼 느껴져 장바구니를 포기하게 하지만, 같은 돈이 더 높은 가격에 숨으면 저항이 적다고 설명한다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about a retailer that sets a minimum order for free shipping?
options: It hopes customers will buy more than they originally intended.
It plans to lose money on every order.
It does not actually charge for any products.
It refuses to ship to distant locations.
questions.explain: 지문은 최소 주문액 방식이 자격을 갖추려고 계획에 없던 물건을 추가하도록 유도한다고 했으므로, 소비자가 더 사기를 바란다고 추론할 수 있다.

title: Restoring the Beaver
passage: For centuries, beavers were trapped nearly to extinction across much of Europe and North America, prized for their fur. Their disappearance changed landscapes in ways few people noticed at the time. Without beavers building dams, streams ran straight and fast, cutting deep channels and rushing water away after every storm. Recently, ecologists have begun reintroducing beavers, and the results have surprised even supporters. The dams these animals build slow the flow of water, spreading it across wide, shallow ponds and soggy meadows. This stored water seeps into the ground, recharging supplies that feed wells and keep streams flowing through dry months. The ponds also trap sediment and create rich habitat for fish, birds, and amphibians. In several regions, areas with beaver dams suffered less damage during floods, because the wetlands absorbed surges that would otherwise have torn through towns. Not everyone welcomes the animals; flooded fields and blocked culverts can frustrate landowners. Still, a growing number of communities now see beavers less as pests than as low-cost engineers whose instinct to dam quietly performs work that would cost millions to replicate.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Beavers should be trapped again for their valuable fur.
Reintroducing beavers can restore wetlands and provide benefits like water storage and flood reduction.
Beavers cause more harm than any other animal.
Streams are healthier when they run straight and fast.
questions.explain: 지문은 비버를 다시 도입하면 습지를 복원하고 물 저장과 홍수 완화 같은 이익을 준다는 점을 중심 내용으로 제시한다.

questions.q: According to the passage, how do beaver dams help during floods?
options: They speed water away from towns.
The wetlands they create absorb surges that would otherwise damage towns.
They block rivers so no water can flow.
They make streams run deeper and faster.
questions.explain: 지문은 비버 댐이 만든 습지가 마을을 휩쓸 물의 급증을 흡수해 홍수 피해를 줄였다고 설명한다.

questions.q: The phrase 'low-cost engineers' is used to suggest that beavers
options: are paid small wages for their work.
naturally perform expensive ecological work for free.
design buildings for human towns.
are too cheap to be effective.
questions.explain: 지문은 비버의 댐 짓는 본능이 수백만 달러가 들 작업을 조용히 수행한다고 했으므로, '저비용 엔지니어'는 값비싼 생태 작업을 공짜로 한다는 의미다.

title: The Mapmaker Marie Tharp
passage: Marie Tharp spent much of her career turning columns of numbers into a picture of a world no one had ever seen. Trained in geology at a time when few women entered the field, she joined a research group studying the ocean floor in the mid-twentieth century. Ships crossed the Atlantic dragging instruments that measured depth, returning with long tables of soundings. Tharp converted these figures into detailed profiles of the seabed, and as she worked, a striking feature emerged: a deep valley running down the center of a vast underwater mountain range. She argued that this rift was evidence the seafloor was splitting apart. At first her interpretation was dismissed by colleagues, including one who called it 'girl talk.' Yet the pattern held across profile after profile, and additional data on earthquakes lined up neatly with the valley she had traced. Her maps, eventually published, helped persuade a skeptical scientific community that the continents move. Tharp received little public credit during the years her work mattered most, but later generations recognized her quiet drawings as a turning point in how we understand the planet.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Marie Tharp invented the instruments used to measure ocean depth.
Marie Tharp's maps of the seafloor revealed evidence that helped confirm the continents move.
Marie Tharp preferred working on land rather than studying the ocean.
Marie Tharp received great public fame early in her career.
questions.explain: 지문은 타프의 해저 지도가 대륙 이동을 입증하는 데 도움이 된 증거를 드러냈다는 점을 중심으로 다룬다.

questions.q: What feature did Tharp identify in her seafloor profiles?
options: A flat plain with no mountains.
A deep valley running down the center of an underwater mountain range.
A series of volcanic islands above the water.
A coral reef circling the Atlantic.
questions.explain: 지문은 타프가 거대한 해저 산맥 중앙을 따라 흐르는 깊은 골짜기를 발견했다고 명시한다.

questions.q: What can be inferred about how Tharp's ideas were initially received?
options: They were immediately accepted by all scientists.
They were doubted at first but later supported by additional data.
They were ignored and never tested.
They were proven completely wrong.
questions.explain: 지문은 동료들이 처음엔 그녀의 해석을 무시했으나 지진 자료가 골짜기와 일치하며 결국 설득력을 얻었다고 서술하므로 이를 추론할 수 있다.

questions.q: The author's attitude toward Marie Tharp can best be described as
options: dismissive and critical
respectful and appreciative
indifferent and neutral
amused and mocking
questions.explain: 지문은 그녀의 작업을 행성 이해의 전환점으로 평가하고 부당한 무시를 언급하며 존중하고 높이 평가하는 태도를 보인다.

title: The Deep-Sea Glow
passage: More than two-thirds of the animals living in the open ocean produce their own light, a phenomenon called bioluminescence. Unlike the warm glow of an electric bulb, this light is cold: nearly all the energy released by the chemical reaction becomes light rather than heat. The reaction depends on a molecule called luciferin, which an enzyme oxidizes to release a flash of blue or green. Marine creatures put this ability to surprisingly varied uses. Some squid release glowing clouds to confuse predators, much as an octopus releases ink. Certain fish carry colonies of luminous bacteria in special pouches, switching the light on or off by covering it with a flap of skin. Others use precisely timed pulses to attract mates in the darkness. Because seawater absorbs red light quickly but lets blue travel far, most ocean light is blue. Researchers studying these signals must therefore design instruments sensitive to a narrow band of color, a constraint that has quietly shaped decades of deep-sea exploration.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Bioluminescence is rare among ocean animals
Many ocean animals make their own light and use it in varied ways
Squid are the only animals that glow
Seawater blocks all colors of light equally
questions.explain: 지문은 바다 동물 다수가 스스로 빛을 내며 그 빛을 다양하게 활용한다는 점을 설명한다.

questions.q: According to the passage, why is most ocean light blue?
options: Blue luciferin is the only kind
Seawater absorbs red quickly but lets blue travel far
Predators cannot see blue
Bacteria only produce blue
questions.explain: 본문은 바닷물이 빨간빛을 빨리 흡수하고 파란빛은 멀리 전달하기 때문이라고 명시한다.

questions.q: It can be inferred that researchers' instruments are tuned to blue-green light because
options: that is the color most ocean signals use
blue is easiest to manufacture
red instruments are too expensive
animals dislike other colors
questions.explain: 바다 신호가 대부분 파란빛이므로 좁은 색 대역에 민감한 기기를 설계해야 한다고 했다.

questions.q: The phrase 'this light is cold' in the passage means that the light
options: feels chilly to the touch
releases almost no heat
appears only in cold water
is dim and faint
questions.explain: 바로 뒤에서 에너지 대부분이 열이 아니라 빛이 된다고 설명하므로 '열이 거의 없다'는 뜻이다.

title: The Cartographer of the Nile
passage: In the second century, a scholar named Claudius Ptolemy compiled a guide to drawing the known world onto a flat surface. Working in Alexandria, he gathered the reports of merchants, sailors, and soldiers, then assigned coordinates of latitude and longitude to thousands of places. His great innovation was not a single map but a method: he proposed mathematical rules for projecting a curved Earth onto a flat sheet without distorting it beyond recognition. For centuries his coordinates guided travelers, even though many were wildly inaccurate, because he had trusted secondhand accounts of distant lands he never visited. When his work was rediscovered in Renaissance Europe, it sparked a wave of new maps, and printers raced to publish editions. Ironically, Ptolemy's mistaken estimate of the Earth's size encouraged explorers to believe Asia lay closer to Europe than it truly was. Thus an ancient error, preserved through careful copying, helped push ships westward across an ocean its author never imagined.

questions.q: What was Ptolemy's principal contribution, according to the passage?
options: He sailed to every place he mapped
He developed a method for projecting a round Earth onto flat sheets
He invented latitude and longitude
He correctly measured the Earth's size
questions.explain: 본문은 그의 핵심 혁신이 둥근 지구를 평면에 투영하는 수학적 방법이었다고 말한다.

questions.q: Why were many of Ptolemy's coordinates inaccurate?
options: He used broken instruments
He relied on secondhand accounts of places he never visited
He copied a rival's maps
He measured only at night
questions.explain: 그가 직접 가보지 않은 먼 땅에 대한 전언을 신뢰했기 때문이라고 명시되어 있다.

questions.q: What is ironic about Ptolemy's error regarding the Earth's size?
options: It made his maps more accurate
A mistake helped encourage westward voyages he never imagined
It proved Asia was unreachable
It was corrected in his own lifetime
questions.explain: 지구 크기를 작게 본 오류가 탐험가들이 서쪽으로 항해하도록 부추겼다는 아이러니를 지문이 강조한다.

title: The Quiet Revolution of the Shipping Container
passage: Before the late 1950s, loading a cargo ship was slow, costly, and chaotic. Dockworkers handled barrels, crates, and sacks one item at a time, and a vessel might sit in port for a week. A trucking entrepreneur named Malcolm McLean wondered why the whole truck trailer could not simply be lifted aboard. From that question grew the standardized steel shipping container, a plain metal box of fixed dimensions that could move seamlessly between ship, train, and truck. The genius lay less in the box itself than in the agreement to make every box the same. Once ports, railways, and shippers adopted identical sizes, cranes could stack and transfer containers with astonishing speed, and the cost of moving goods plummeted. Cheaper transport made it practical to manufacture parts in one country and assemble them in another, knitting together a global economy. Today the humble container is so ordinary that few travelers notice the stacks at any port, yet this unremarkable box reshaped where and how the world makes nearly everything.

questions.q: According to the passage, where did the real genius of the container lie?
options: In the strength of the steel
In the agreement to standardize every box's size
In McLean's trucking company
In faster ships
questions.explain: 본문은 천재성이 상자 자체보다 모든 상자를 같은 규격으로 만들기로 한 합의에 있었다고 한다.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Dockworkers preferred barrels to boxes
A standardized container quietly transformed global trade
Shipping has always been efficient
McLean failed to change shipping
questions.explain: 지문은 표준화된 컨테이너가 조용히 세계 무역을 바꿨다는 것이 핵심이다.

questions.q: It can be inferred that the container made global manufacturing networks possible because
options: it made transport cheap enough to spread production across countries
it forced all factories into one nation
it eliminated the need for ships
it raised shipping costs sharply
questions.explain: 운송비가 급락해 여러 나라에 생산을 분산하는 것이 실용적이 되었다고 본문이 설명한다.

title: Why Crowds Are Sometimes Wise
passage: In 1906, a statistician attending a country fair watched hundreds of people guess the weight of an ox. No single villager knew the answer, and the individual guesses ranged widely. Yet when he averaged all the guesses, the result fell within one pound of the ox's true weight. This surprising accuracy, later called the wisdom of crowds, occurs only under specific conditions. The guessers must be diverse, so their errors point in different directions and cancel out. They must also judge independently, without copying their neighbors, because shared influence makes the whole group lean the same wrong way. Finally, there must be some means of combining the answers, such as averaging. When any of these conditions fails, the crowd can grow foolish rather than wise: panics, fads, and bubbles all arise when people imitate one another instead of judging for themselves. The lesson is subtle. A group is not magically smart; it is smart only when its members think apart and pool the results.

questions.q: What is the central claim of the passage?
options: Crowds are always smarter than individuals
Crowds are wise only under specific conditions
Averaging guesses never works
Imitation makes crowds wise
questions.explain: 지문의 핵심은 군중이 특정 조건이 충족될 때만 현명하다는 것이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, which condition prevents the crowd from leaning the same wrong way?
options: Everyone copying a leader
Members judging independently
Excluding diverse opinions
Avoiding any averaging
questions.explain: 서로 베끼지 않고 독립적으로 판단해야 집단이 같은 오류로 기울지 않는다고 했다.

questions.q: From the passage, it can be inferred that financial bubbles occur when
options: people judge independently
people imitate one another instead of thinking for themselves
guesses are averaged carefully
crowds remain diverse
questions.explain: 패닉, 유행, 거품은 사람들이 스스로 판단하지 않고 서로 모방할 때 생긴다고 본문이 밝힌다.

questions.q: The author's tone in the final two sentences is best described as
options: scornful
measured and instructive
fearful
indifferent
questions.explain: 마지막 두 문장은 교훈을 차분히 정리해 설명하는 신중하고 교훈적인 어조다.

title: The Paradox of Thrift
passage: Saving money is usually praised as prudent, and for a single household it almost always is. Spend less than you earn, and your savings cushion you against hard times. Yet economists point to a curious puzzle that appears when everyone saves at once. If all households suddenly cut spending to build savings, the shops they would have patronized see falling sales. Those shops then order fewer goods, factories trim production, and workers lose income. With less income, people can save even less than before, and total savings may actually shrink. This is the paradox of thrift: behavior that is sensible for one person can be harmful when adopted by all simultaneously. The puzzle matters most during downturns, when fear spreads and many people tighten their belts together. Some economists argue this is precisely when governments should spend, stepping in to replace the demand that anxious households withdraw. Others worry such spending merely delays a needed adjustment. The debate, decades old, remains unsettled because the economy rarely repeats itself exactly.

questions.q: What does the 'paradox of thrift' describe?
options: Saving is always harmful
Behavior sensible for one person can harm everyone if all do it at once
Households should never save
Governments should never spend
questions.explain: 절약의 역설은 개인에게 합리적인 행동이 모두가 동시에 하면 해로울 수 있다는 것이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, what happens first when all households cut spending?
options: Factories hire more workers
Shops see falling sales
Savings immediately grow
Wages rise
questions.explain: 모두가 지출을 줄이면 가게들의 매출이 떨어지는 일이 먼저 일어난다고 했다.

questions.q: It can be inferred that the paradox is most dangerous when
options: the economy is booming
fear leads many people to cut spending together
only one household saves
factories expand
questions.explain: 공포가 퍼져 많은 이가 함께 허리띠를 졸라매는 침체기에 이 역설이 가장 문제된다고 명시한다.

title: Bringing Back the Beaver
passage: For most of the twentieth century, beavers were treated as nuisances. Trappers had nearly wiped them out, and the few that remained were often removed for flooding fields and blocking culverts. Recently, however, ecologists have begun to see the animal as an ally. A beaver dam slows a rushing stream, spreading water across a valley floor. The resulting wetland stores water during dry spells, filters out pollutants, and creates habitat for fish, frogs, and birds. In regions prone to wildfire, the moist green strips around beaver ponds can act as natural firebreaks, refusing to burn even when surrounding forest is scorched. Some land managers now deliberately relocate beavers into damaged watersheds, a practice once unthinkable. The animals rebuild in weeks what engineers would spend years and fortunes to construct. There are trade-offs, of course: a beaver cannot read property lines, and its ponds may flood a road or a pasture. Yet a growing number of scientists argue that learning to live alongside this stubborn engineer is cheaper and wiser than fighting it.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Beavers should be trapped to extinction
Beavers, once seen as pests, are now valued for restoring watersheds
Beaver dams cause only harm
Engineers build better dams than beavers
questions.explain: 지문은 한때 해로운 동물로 여겨진 비버가 이제 수계 복원에 가치 있는 존재로 재평가된다는 것이 핵심이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, how can beaver ponds help during wildfires?
options: They spread the flames
Their moist green strips can act as firebreaks
They dry out the forest
They attract lightning
questions.explain: 비버 연못 주변의 촉촉한 녹지대가 천연 방화선 역할을 한다고 본문이 설명한다.

questions.q: The phrase 'a beaver cannot read property lines' is used to suggest that
options: beavers are intelligent surveyors
beavers may flood land regardless of human boundaries
beavers avoid roads carefully
beavers respect pastures
questions.explain: 비버가 인간의 경계와 무관하게 도로나 목초지를 물에 잠기게 할 수 있음을 비유적으로 나타낸다.

questions.q: The author's overall attitude toward beavers is best described as
options: hostile
cautiously appreciative
indifferent
alarmed
questions.explain: 단점을 인정하면서도 비버와 공존하는 편이 현명하다고 보는 신중하지만 호의적인 태도다.

title: The Mathematician Who Coded by Hand
passage: Long before electronic computers existed, Ada Lovelace imagined what they might one day do. The daughter of a famous poet, she was steered toward mathematics by a mother who feared she might inherit her father's restless temperament. In the 1840s, Lovelace studied the plans for a mechanical calculating engine designed by her friend Charles Babbage, a machine never fully built in their lifetimes. Translating a French article about the engine, she added notes longer than the original text. In them she described, step by step, how the machine could compute a complicated sequence of numbers, a procedure many historians regard as the first published algorithm intended for a machine. More striking still, she speculated that such a device might someday manipulate symbols other than numbers, perhaps even composing music, if the rules were expressed correctly. Babbage thought mainly of arithmetic; Lovelace glimpsed something broader. She did not live to see her vision realized, dying at thirty-six, yet her notes anticipated ideas that would not flower for another century.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Lovelace built the first computer
Lovelace foresaw broad uses of computing long before machines existed
Babbage wrote the first algorithm
Lovelace disliked mathematics
questions.explain: 지문은 기계가 존재하기 전에 러브레이스가 컴퓨팅의 넓은 가능성을 내다봤다는 점을 핵심으로 한다.

questions.q: According to the passage, how did Lovelace's vision differ from Babbage's?
options: She cared only about poetry
She imagined the machine handling symbols beyond numbers, even music
She rejected the engine entirely
She thought only of arithmetic
questions.explain: 배비지는 주로 산술을 생각했지만 러브레이스는 숫자 외 기호, 심지어 음악까지 다룰 수 있다고 상상했다.

questions.q: It can be inferred that Lovelace's notes were significant because
options: they were shorter than the original article
they anticipated ideas realized only a century later
they described how to build the machine cheaply
they proved Babbage wrong about mathematics
questions.explain: 그녀의 주석이 한 세기 뒤에야 꽃피울 개념을 앞서 예견했다고 본문이 밝힌다.

title: Why the Sky Is Blue
passage: Sunlight appears white, but it is actually a mixture of all the colors of the visible spectrum, each traveling as a wave of a different length. When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, which are far smaller than the wavelengths of visible light. These tiny molecules scatter shorter wavelengths much more strongly than longer ones, a relationship first described by the physicist Lord Rayleigh. Because blue and violet light have the shortest wavelengths, they are scattered across the sky in every direction, reaching our eyes from all angles. The sky looks blue rather than violet partly because the sun emits less violet light and partly because human eyes are more sensitive to blue. At sunset, sunlight travels through a thicker layer of atmosphere, so most of the blue has already been scattered away before the light reaches us, leaving the reds and oranges that paint the horizon.

questions.q: The main idea of this passage is that
options: violet light is scattered more than any other color across the sky
Lord Rayleigh discovered all the colors of the visible spectrum
the sky's color results from the scattering of shorter wavelengths of sunlight by air molecules
sunlight appears white because it contains no blue or violet light
questions.explain: 지문 전체가 햇빛의 짧은 파장이 공기 분자에 의해 산란되어 하늘색이 만들어지는 과정을 설명하므로 'the scattering of shorter wavelengths of sunlight by air molecules'가 정답이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, the nitrogen and oxygen molecules in the atmosphere are
options: much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light
larger than the wavelengths of blue light
unable to scatter any visible light
the source of the sun's violet light
questions.explain: 지문에서 질소와 산소 분자가 '가시광선의 파장보다 훨씬 작다(far smaller than the wavelengths of visible light)'고 했으므로 'much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light'가 정답이다.

questions.q: In this passage, the word "scattered" most nearly means
options: absorbed and destroyed
reflected back into space
combined into white light
redirected in many directions
questions.explain: 지문에서 빛이 '사방으로 산란되어(scattered across the sky in every direction)' 눈에 도달한다고 했으므로 'redirected in many directions'가 정답이다.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that sunsets appear red because
options: the sun produces more red light in the evening
blue light is scattered away over the longer path through the atmosphere
human eyes lose their sensitivity to blue at night
the atmosphere becomes thinner near the horizon
questions.explain: 지문에서 일몰 때 빛이 더 두꺼운 대기를 지나며 파란색이 이미 산란되어 사라진다고 했으므로 'blue light is scattered away over the longer path'가 정답이다.

title: How Soap Cleans
passage: Water alone struggles to remove greasy dirt because oil and water do not mix. Soap solves this problem through molecules that have a split personality: one end is attracted to water, while the other end is attracted to oil and grease. Chemists call the water-loving end hydrophilic and the oil-loving end hydrophobic. When soap is added to water, its molecules surround a droplet of grease, pointing their oil-loving ends inward toward the grease and their water-loving ends outward toward the surrounding water. These tiny clusters, called micelles, trap the grease in their centers and lift it away from skin or fabric. Because the outer surface of each micelle is attracted to water, the whole package can be rinsed away easily. This is why washing with soap removes oily grime that plain water leaves behind. The same principle allows detergents to clean dishes and laundry, breaking up fats that water cannot dissolve on its own.

questions.q: The main idea of this passage is that
options: detergents are always more effective than soap at cleaning laundry
soap cleans by using molecules that bond to both water and grease
oil and water can be made to mix together permanently
micelles are harmful clusters that trap dirt on the skin
questions.explain: 지문은 비누 분자가 물과 기름 양쪽에 결합해 때를 제거한다고 설명하므로 'molecules that bond to both water and grease'가 정답이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, a micelle is
options: a molecule that has only a water-loving end
a type of grease that resists soap
the water-loving end of a single soap molecule
a cluster of soap molecules surrounding a droplet of grease
questions.explain: 지문에서 미셀은 '기름 방울을 둘러싼 비누 분자 무리(clusters ... surround a droplet of grease)'라고 했으므로 'a cluster of soap molecules surrounding a droplet of grease'가 정답이다.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that plain water fails to remove oily dirt because
options: water and oil do not mix, so water cannot surround the grease by itself
water dissolves grease too quickly to be rinsed away
water molecules are naturally hydrophobic
water forms micelles that trap clean particles instead
questions.explain: 지문에서 기름과 물이 섞이지 않기 때문에 물만으로는 기름때를 제거하지 못한다고 했으므로 'water and oil do not mix'가 정답이다.

questions.q: In this passage, the word "hydrophobic" most nearly means
options: strongly attracted to water
capable of dissolving salt
tending to avoid water
electrically charged
questions.explain: 지문에서 hydrophobic은 기름을 좋아하는(oil-loving) 끝을 가리키며 물에 이끌리지 않으므로 'tending to avoid water'가 정답이다.

title: Why Iron Rusts
passage: Rust is the familiar reddish-brown crust that forms on iron and steel left exposed to the elements. It is the product of a chemical reaction called oxidation, in which iron combines with oxygen in the presence of water to form iron oxide. Both moisture and oxygen must be present for rust to develop, which is why iron corrodes quickly in humid air but remains stable in a dry desert or sealed underwater without dissolved oxygen. Unlike the protective coating that forms on aluminum, rust is flaky and porous, so it does not shield the metal beneath. Instead, it peels away and exposes fresh iron to further attack, allowing corrosion to eat steadily into the object. Engineers combat rust in several ways: painting or oiling the surface to block moisture, coating steel with zinc in a process called galvanizing, or blending iron with chromium to make stainless steel. Each method works by keeping oxygen and water from reaching the vulnerable iron.

questions.q: The main idea of this passage is that
options: rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water, and it can be prevented by blocking them
aluminum is a stronger metal than iron in every condition
galvanizing is the only reliable way to stop corrosion
iron corrodes fastest when it is sealed underwater
questions.explain: 지문은 녹이 철과 산소·물의 반응으로 생기며 이를 차단해 막을 수 있다고 설명하므로 'rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water, and it can be prevented by blocking them'이 정답이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, iron remains stable when
options: it is exposed to humid air
it is coated with flaky iron oxide
it is kept in a dry environment or water without dissolved oxygen
both oxygen and moisture are present around it
questions.explain: 지문에서 철은 건조한 사막이나 용존 산소가 없는 물속에서 안정적이라고 했으므로 'a dry environment or water without dissolved oxygen'이 정답이다.

questions.q: The author's primary purpose in this passage is to
options: warn readers about the dangers of living in humid climates
explain what causes rust and how it can be prevented
argue that stainless steel is superior to all other metals
compare the history of iron and aluminum production
questions.explain: 지문의 목적은 녹의 원인과 예방법을 설명하는 것이므로 'explain what causes rust and how it can be prevented'가 정답이다.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that the coating on aluminum differs from rust because it
options: forms much faster than rust does
is also flaky and porous
requires no oxygen in order to form
protects the metal underneath from further corrosion
questions.explain: 지문에서 알루미늄의 보호막과 달리 녹은 속 금속을 보호하지 못한다고 했으므로, 그 보호막은 'protects the metal underneath from further corrosion'이 정답이다.

title: How Caves Form
passage: Many of the world's largest caves are carved not by rushing rivers but by a slow chemical process acting on limestone. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil, forming a weak carbonic acid. As this mildly acidic water seeps through cracks in limestone bedrock, it gradually dissolves the rock, widening the cracks into passages over thousands of years. Landscapes shaped this way, riddled with caves, sinkholes, and underground streams, are known as karst. Once a cavern opens and drains of water, a second process begins. Water dripping from the ceiling leaves behind tiny deposits of dissolved mineral, slowly building icicle-shaped stalactites that hang downward. Drips that strike the floor build stalagmites upward from below. Given enough time, a stalactite and a stalagmite may join into a single column. Because these formations grow only a fraction of an inch per century, the elaborate chambers found in limestone caves record tens of thousands of years of patient mineral deposition.

questions.q: The main idea of this passage is that
options: stalactites grow much faster than stalagmites in most caves
rushing rivers are the main force that carves large caves
karst landscapes are found only where rivers flow underground
limestone caves and their formations are created by the slow chemical action of acidic water over long periods
questions.explain: 지문은 석회암 동굴과 그 형성물이 산성 물의 느린 화학작용으로 오랜 시간에 걸쳐 만들어진다고 설명하므로 'created by the slow chemical action of acidic water over long periods'가 정답이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, the acid that dissolves limestone forms when
options: underground streams mix with seawater
rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil
minerals drip from the cave ceiling
a stalactite joins with a stalagmite
questions.explain: 지문에서 빗물이 공기와 토양의 이산화탄소를 흡수해 약한 탄산이 된다고 했으므로 'rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil'가 정답이다.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that a cave's mineral formations begin to grow
options: before the limestone bedrock develops any cracks
only while rushing water still fills the chamber
after the cavern has drained of water
faster than the surrounding rock dissolves
questions.explain: 지문에서 '동굴이 열리고 물이 빠진 뒤(Once a cavern opens and drains of water)' 두 번째 과정이 시작된다고 했으므로 'after the cavern has drained of water'가 정답이다.

questions.q: In this passage, the word "seeps" most nearly means
options: trickles slowly
evaporates completely
freezes solid
bubbles violently
questions.explain: 지문에서 산성 물이 바위 틈으로 천천히 스며든다는 맥락이므로 'trickles slowly'가 정답이다.

title: How Clouds Form
passage: Clouds form when warm, moist air rises and cools. Air near the ground absorbs water that evaporates from oceans, lakes, and plants, holding it as invisible water vapor. Warm air can carry more of this vapor than cold air can. When a parcel of warm air rises, it expands and cools as the surrounding pressure drops, and eventually it reaches a temperature at which it can no longer hold all its moisture. At that point, called the dew point, the vapor begins to condense into countless tiny droplets. These droplets do not form on their own; they gather around microscopic particles of dust, salt, or smoke known as condensation nuclei. Billions of such droplets together become visible as a cloud. Whether a cloud produces rain depends on whether its droplets grow large and heavy enough to fall. Meteorologists read the shapes and heights of clouds as clues to the movements of air and the weather that may follow.

questions.q: The main idea of this passage is that
options: clouds are made of invisible water vapor
cold air can hold more moisture than warm air
clouds form when rising warm air cools and its water vapor condenses around tiny particles
meteorologists can prevent rain by studying the shapes of clouds
questions.explain: 지문은 상승한 따뜻한 공기가 식으며 수증기가 미세 입자 주위에 응결해 구름이 생긴다고 설명하므로 'rising warm air cools and its water vapor condenses around tiny particles'가 정답이다.

questions.q: According to the passage, condensation nuclei are
options: microscopic particles around which water droplets gather
large raindrops that fall from a cloud
pockets of warm air that rise from the ground
the temperature at which vapor begins to condense
questions.explain: 지문에서 응결핵은 물방울이 그 주위에 모이는 미세한 입자라고 했으므로 'microscopic particles around which water droplets gather'가 정답이다.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that a cloud will most likely produce rain when
options: its droplets remain small and light
its droplets grow large and heavy enough to fall
the air around it cools to the dew point
no condensation nuclei are present in the air
questions.explain: 지문에서 비는 물방울이 떨어질 만큼 크고 무거워질 때 내린다고 했으므로 'its droplets grow large and heavy enough to fall'이 정답이다.

questions.q: The author's primary purpose in this passage is to
options: persuade readers to study meteorology as a career
compare the different types of clouds by their shape
warn readers about the dangers of severe storms
explain the process by which clouds form
questions.explain: 지문의 목적은 구름이 형성되는 과정을 설명하는 것이므로 'explain the process by which clouds form'이 정답이다.

title: The Science of Lightning
passage: Lightning is a sudden discharge of electricity within a storm cloud or between a cloud and the ground. Inside a towering thundercloud, powerful air currents hurl ice crystals and water droplets against one another. These collisions strip away electric charge, leaving lighter particles positively charged near the top of the cloud and heavier ones negatively charged near the bottom. When the difference in charge grows large enough to overcome the air's resistance, electricity leaps across the gap in a brilliant flash, heating the surrounding air to roughly five times the temperature of the sun's surface. This abrupt heating makes the air expand explosively, producing the shock wave we hear as thunder. Because light travels far faster than sound, we see the flash almost instantly but hear the thunder later. Counting the seconds between them offers a rough estimate of a storm's distance: sound covers about one mile every five seconds, so a ten-second gap places the strike two miles away.

questions.q: The main idea of this passage is that
options: thunder is far more dangerous to people than lightning

title: How Water Climbs a Tree
passage: A tall tree faces a daily engineering challenge: lifting water from its roots to leaves that may stand hundreds of feet above the ground, without any pump. The solution relies on the peculiar properties of water and the structure of the tree. Water travels upward through narrow tubes called xylem, which run from the roots to the leaves like a bundle of drinking straws. In the leaves, water evaporates from tiny pores and escapes into the air, a process called transpiration. As each water molecule leaves, it tugs on the molecules behind it, because water molecules cling to one another through a force called cohesion. This creates an unbroken chain of tension that pulls the entire column upward, much like sipping through a straw. The dry air outside effectively does the pulling. Remarkably, this passive system requires no energy from the tree itself, allowing the tallest trees on Earth to move hundreds of gallons of water on a warm day.

options: trees move water upward without a pump by relying on evaporation and the cohesion of water molecules

title: Why Ice Floats
passage: Most substances grow denser as they freeze, so their solid form sinks in the liquid. Water is a striking exception: ice floats. The reason lies in the shape of the water molecule and the way its molecules bond. Each water molecule can form links called hydrogen bonds with its neighbors. In liquid water, molecules slide close together and constantly rearrange. But as water freezes, these hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open, six-sided crystal lattice that holds them farther apart than they sit in the liquid. Because the same number of molecules occupies more space, ice is about nine percent less dense than the water beneath it, so it rises to the surface. This quirk has profound consequences for life. When a lake freezes, a layer of ice forms on top and insulates the water below, allowing fish and other organisms to survive the winter. Were ice to sink instead, ponds and lakes could freeze solid from the bottom up.

questions.explain: 지문에서 얼음은 아래 물보다 약 9% 밀도가 낮다고 했으므로 'less dense than the water beneath it'가 정답이다.

title: How Microwave Ovens Heat Food
passage: A microwave oven cooks food in a way fundamentally different from a conventional oven, which surrounds food with hot air. At the heart of a microwave sits a device called a magnetron, which generates microwaves — a form of electromagnetic radiation — at a specific frequency. These microwaves pass into the cooking chamber and are absorbed by water molecules in the food. A water molecule has a positive end and a negative end, so it twists back and forth to align with the rapidly reversing electric field of the microwaves, flipping billions of times each second. This frantic motion is simply heat: as the molecules jostle their neighbors, the food's temperature rises. Because the waves penetrate an inch or two beyond the surface, microwaves heat food faster than an oven that must warm it from the outside in. It also explains why foods high in water heat quickly, while a dry ceramic plate stays relatively cool, warming mainly through contact with the food it holds.

title: The Rock Cycle
passage: Geologists group rocks into three families based on how they form, and the rock cycle describes how one type can slowly transform into another. Igneous rock forms when molten material from within the Earth cools and hardens, either underground or after erupting as lava. Exposed at the surface, rock is broken down by wind, water, and ice into sediment. When layers of this sediment are buried and compressed over long ages, they cement together into sedimentary rock, which often preserves fossils. If existing rock is subjected to intense heat and pressure deep underground without melting, its minerals recrystallize into metamorphic rock. Should that rock sink deep enough to melt entirely, it becomes magma once more, ready to cool into new igneous rock and begin the journey again. No single pathway is fixed; a metamorphic rock might erode into sediment rather than melt. Driven by heat from Earth's interior and the energy of sun and gravity at the surface, the cycle turns over millions of years.

title: How Fossils Form
passage: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms, yet the vast majority of living things never become fossils at all. When a plant or animal dies, scavengers, bacteria, and weather usually break it down within a short time. Fossilization becomes possible only when an organism is buried quickly, often by mud or sand at the bottom of a lake or sea, which shields it from decay and oxygen. Soft tissues almost always rot away, so most fossils preserve only hard parts such as bones, shells, and teeth. In the most common process, called permineralization, groundwater seeps into the tiny pores of buried bone and deposits dissolved minerals, gradually turning the remains to stone while keeping their original shape. Not all fossils are body parts; footprints, burrows, and even preserved droppings record behavior and are known as trace fossils. Because the conditions required are so specific, the fossil record captures only a small and uneven sample of the life that once existed.

title: The Science of Hibernation
passage: Hibernation is a survival strategy that allows certain animals to endure winters when food is scarce and temperatures drop. Far more than ordinary sleep, true hibernation involves a dramatic slowing of the body. A hibernating ground squirrel, for example, may let its body temperature fall to near freezing, its heartbeat slow from hundreds of beats per minute to just a few, and its breathing nearly stop. These changes cut the animal's energy needs to a tiny fraction of normal, letting it live for months on fat reserves built up during autumn. Because its metabolism runs so slowly, the animal neither eats nor drinks throughout the winter. Hibernators do not stay dormant continuously; they periodically warm up and rouse for brief periods before sinking back down. Notably, bears are lighter hibernators than often assumed, lowering their temperature only modestly and waking more readily. When spring returns and food becomes available again, the animal gradually restores its normal body temperature and activity.

title: The Physics of Friction
passage: Friction is the force that resists motion when two surfaces are in contact. Although a tabletop may look and feel smooth, under a microscope its surface is a landscape of microscopic ridges and valleys. When one surface slides over another, these irregularities catch and drag, and tiny points of contact briefly stick together, all of which oppose movement. Friction can be a nuisance or an ally. It wears down machine parts and wastes energy as heat, which is why engineers lubricate engines with oil to reduce it. Yet without friction, walking would be impossible, since our feet rely on grip against the ground, and cars could neither accelerate nor brake. Generally, it takes a larger force to start an object sliding than to keep it moving, because the surfaces settle into each other when at rest. Rougher surfaces and heavier loads increase friction, while smooth surfaces, wheels, and lubricants reduce it, allowing objects to move with far less effort.

title: How Refrigerators Stay Cold
passage: A refrigerator does not create cold; it moves heat from inside the cabinet to the room outside. This seemingly backward feat is accomplished by a circulating fluid called a refrigerant, which is chosen because it boils and condenses at convenient temperatures. Inside the appliance, the refrigerant passes through a set of coils where it evaporates, and evaporation absorbs heat, drawing warmth out of the food compartment. A compressor then squeezes the now-gaseous refrigerant, raising its pressure and temperature. The hot, compressed gas flows through condenser coils on the back or bottom of the refrigerator, where it releases its heat into the kitchen and condenses back into a liquid. The cooled liquid then returns to begin the cycle again. This is why the coils behind a refrigerator feel warm to the touch and why a refrigerator actually adds heat to a closed kitchen overall. The same basic cycle, run in reverse, allows a heat pump to warm a house in winter.

title: The Printing Revolution
passage: In the mid-fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith working in the German city of Mainz, developed a printing system based on movable metal type. His method combined durable individual letters that could be rearranged and reused, an oil-based ink that adhered well to metal, and a modified screw press similar to those used for pressing grapes. Before this innovation, European books were copied by hand, a slow and costly process that kept them scarce and confined largely to monasteries, universities, and wealthy patrons. Printing changed the situation with remarkable speed. By 1500, presses operated in hundreds of European towns, and historians estimate that millions of volumes had been produced. Cheaper and more plentiful books widened access to religious texts, scientific treatises, and practical manuals, encouraging literacy among merchants and artisans. Although Gutenberg himself earned little wealth from his invention, the technology he assembled transformed how information circulated in Europe and beyond.

title: Routes of the Silk Road
passage: The Silk Road was not a single highway but a shifting network of caravan tracks and sea lanes that linked China with Central Asia, India, Persia, and the Mediterranean world. Overland exchange along these routes expanded during the second century BCE, after the Han dynasty sent the envoy Zhang Qian westward and later secured corridors through Central Asia. Chinese silk gave the network its modern name, coined by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in the nineteenth century, but traders also carried spices, glassware, precious metals, and horses. Few merchants traveled the entire distance; instead, goods passed through many hands, rising in price at each stage. The routes carried more than merchandise. Buddhism spread from India into China along them, papermaking techniques moved westward, and disease-causing microbes traveled with the caravans as well. By connecting distant societies that rarely met face to face, the Silk Road shaped economies and cultures across Eurasia for well over a thousand years.

title: Britain's Industrial Takeoff
passage: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain during the second half of the eighteenth century, and its earliest transformations appeared in the manufacture of cloth. Inventions such as James Hargreaves's spinning jenny and Richard Arkwright's water frame allowed a single worker to spin many threads at once, while James Watt's improved steam engine eventually freed factories from their dependence on flowing rivers for power. Production moved out of rural cottages, where families had spun and woven at their own pace, and into mills where machines set the rhythm of labor. Cities such as Manchester grew rapidly as workers migrated in search of factory wages, often enduring crowded housing and long shifts. Britain's abundant coal and iron, its navigable rivers, its colonial markets, and its relatively stable banks all helped explain why industrialization took hold there first. Over the following century, the new methods of production spread to continental Europe and North America, remaking economies that had rested on farming for millennia.

title: Joining the Rails
passage: On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in the Utah Territory, a ceremonial golden spike joined the tracks of the Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads, completing the first rail line to span the continental United States. Congress had authorized the project during the Civil War through the Pacific Railway Act of 1862, granting both companies public land and government loans for each mile of track laid. The Central Pacific built eastward from Sacramento, relying heavily on thousands of Chinese laborers who graded roadbeds and bored tunnels through the Sierra Nevada, often in severe winter conditions. The Union Pacific pushed westward across the plains from Omaha with crews that included many Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. Once the line opened, a journey between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts that had previously required months by wagon or ship could be completed in about a week. The railroad accelerated western settlement, expanded national markets, and intensified pressure on the Native American nations of the interior.

title: The Marshall Plan
passage: In June 1947, Secretary of State George C. Marshall used a commencement address at Harvard University to propose that the United States help finance the reconstruction of a Europe still shattered by the Second World War. Factories lay in ruins, currencies had lost much of their value, and food and fuel remained scarce two years after the fighting ended. Congress approved the resulting European Recovery Program, widely known as the Marshall Plan, in 1948. Over roughly four years, the United States provided about thirteen billion dollars in grants and goods to Western European nations, which used the aid to rebuild industry, modernize equipment, and stabilize their finances. American policymakers argued that reviving European economies would create reliable trading partners and reduce the appeal of communist parties in countries facing hardship. The Soviet Union refused to participate and barred the Eastern European states under its influence from doing so, deepening the division of the continent that defined the early Cold War.

title: The Renaissance and Its Reach
passage: The Renaissance, a cultural movement whose name means rebirth, emerged in the city-states of northern Italy during the fourteenth century and gradually spread across Europe. Wealthy commercial centers such as Florence produced merchant and banking families, most famously the Medici, who spent lavishly to commission paintings, sculpture, and architecture. Scholars known as humanists recovered and studied ancient Greek and Roman texts, prizing them as models of eloquence and guides to wise living, and they promoted an education based on grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry, and moral philosophy. Artists including Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo combined close observation of nature with classical ideals of proportion, producing works of striking realism. Renaissance thinkers did not abandon Christianity; rather, most sought to reconcile classical learning with their faith. Aided later by the printing press, which carried new texts and ideas far beyond Italy, the movement reshaped literature, art, and scholarship in France, England, the Netherlands, and the German lands by the sixteenth century.

title: The Erie Canal's Gamble
passage: When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it created a continuous water route between the Atlantic port of New York City and the Great Lakes. The artificial waterway stretched 363 miles across New York State, from the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo, and a series of stone locks lifted boats over an elevation change of more than five hundred feet. Skeptics had mocked the project as Clinton's Ditch, after Governor DeWitt Clinton, its most persistent champion, yet toll revenue repaid the construction debt within about a decade. The canal cut the cost of moving freight between Buffalo and New York City by roughly ninety percent and reduced travel time from weeks to days. Farm products from the interior flowed east while manufactured goods and settlers moved west, and towns such as Rochester and Syracuse flourished along the route. The canal's success helped secure New York City's position as the nation's busiest port and inspired a wave of canal building in other states.

title: Japan's Meiji Transformation
passage: In 1868, a coalition of samurai from domains hostile to the Tokugawa shogunate overthrew that military government and declared the restoration of imperial rule under a teenage emperor who took the reign name Meiji, meaning enlightened rule. The new leadership, alarmed by the Western navies that had forced Japan to open its ports in the 1850s, concluded that only rapid modernization could preserve the country's independence. Within a generation, the government abolished the feudal domains, ended the samurai's hereditary privileges, and built a national army based on conscription. It constructed railroads and telegraph lines, created a system of compulsory education, and sent students and officials abroad to study Western science, industry, and law. In 1889, Japan adopted a written constitution that established an elected assembly, though real power remained with a small circle of oligarchs. By the early twentieth century, Japan had become the first Asian nation to industrialize on a large scale, startling the world with its victory over Russia in 1905.

title: Black Blizzards on the Plains
passage: During the 1930s, a prolonged drought struck the southern Great Plains, a region spanning parts of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico. In the preceding decades, farmers encouraged by high wheat prices had plowed up millions of acres of native grassland whose deep roots had anchored the soil. When the rains failed and crops withered, winds lifted the exposed topsoil into towering dust storms that residents called black blizzards; the storm of April 14, 1935, turned day into night and gave Black Sunday its name. Dust buried fences and machinery, sickened people and livestock, and drifted as far east as the Atlantic coast. Unable to raise crops or pay debts, hundreds of thousands of residents left the region, many following highways west to California. The federal government responded by creating the Soil Conservation Service, which promoted contour plowing and other protective techniques, and by planting rows of trees as windbreaks, efforts that helped reduce erosion when rain finally returned near the decade's end.

title: The Columbian Exchange
passage: Historians use the term Columbian Exchange to describe the vast transfer of plants, animals, people, and microbes between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres that followed Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage; the phrase was popularized by the historian Alfred Crosby in 1972. Crops first domesticated in the Americas, including maize, potatoes, tomatoes, and cacao, crossed the Atlantic and gradually transformed diets in Europe, Africa, and Asia, with the hardy potato supporting population growth in northern Europe. Traveling in the opposite direction, Europeans carried wheat, sugarcane, and livestock such as horses, cattle, and pigs to the Americas, where the horse eventually reshaped hunting and warfare for many peoples of the Great Plains. The exchange also proved catastrophic in one respect: diseases such as smallpox and measles, long established in the Old World, swept through Indigenous American communities that lacked prior exposure, causing population losses on a scale rarely matched in history. The Columbian Exchange thus linked the hemispheres' ecologies and economies while devastating many of the Americas' original societies.

title: The Louisiana Bargain
passage: In 1803, the United States purchased the Louisiana Territory from France for fifteen million dollars, acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles and nearly doubling the nation's size. President Thomas Jefferson had originally sent envoys to Paris hoping only to buy New Orleans, whose port controlled the mouth of the Mississippi River, the outlet through which western farmers shipped their produce. Napoleon Bonaparte, however, offered the entire territory. A revolution by enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue had destroyed his army there and wrecked his plans for an American empire, and with renewed war against Britain approaching, he preferred to sell a distant possession and fill his treasury. Jefferson privately doubted that the Constitution authorized such an acquisition, since the document nowhere mentioned purchasing territory, but the Senate ratified the treaty in October 1803. To learn what the nation had bought, Jefferson dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, whose expedition of 1804 to 1806 mapped rivers, recorded unfamiliar plants and animals, and met Native American nations across the West.

title: Aftermath of the Black Death
passage: In 1347, ships arriving at Sicilian ports from the Black Sea region carried a deadly disease that later generations would call the Black Death. Within about four years, the plague spread across nearly all of Europe, and historians estimate that it killed between one-third and one-half of the continent's population. The disease, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and spread primarily through the bites of infected fleas, produced painful swellings and high fevers and often killed its victims within days. The demographic catastrophe transformed the world of the survivors. With laborers suddenly scarce, peasants and artisans demanded higher wages and greater freedom, and although governments such as England's tried to freeze wages by law, the long-term bargaining power of ordinary workers rose. Landlords in western Europe increasingly leased land for money rents rather than labor services, weakening the institution of serfdom. The plague returned repeatedly for centuries, but no later European outbreak matched the scale of the initial catastrophe of 1347 to 1351.

title: Sputnik and the Space Race
passage: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, a polished metal sphere about the size of a beach ball that circled Earth roughly every ninety-six minutes while transmitting a steady radio beep. Amateur radio operators around the world tuned in, and many Americans reacted with alarm, reasoning that a rocket powerful enough to orbit a satellite could presumably deliver a nuclear warhead across continents. The launch punctured widespread assumptions of American technological superiority, and Washington responded on several fronts. In 1958, Congress created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration to direct civilian spaceflight and passed the National Defense Education Act, which poured federal money into the teaching of science, mathematics, and foreign languages. The rivalry that followed, often called the Space Race, produced a rapid series of milestones, including the first human spaceflight by the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin in 1961, and culminated in the American Apollo 11 mission, which landed astronauts on the Moon in July 1969.

title: The Road to the Nineteenth Amendment
passage: The organized movement for women's voting rights in the United States is often dated to the 1848 convention at Seneca Falls, New York, where reformers including Elizabeth Cady Stanton issued a declaration demanding, among other rights, access to the ballot. For decades afterward, suffragists lectured, petitioned, and organized, winning their earliest full victories in the West; Wyoming enfranchised women in 1869, while it was still a territory. In the 1910s the campaign advanced on two tracks. The National American Woman Suffrage Association, led by Carrie Chapman Catt, combined state-by-state campaigns with lobbying for a federal amendment, while Alice Paul's National Woman's Party staged parades and picketed the White House, where some demonstrators were arrested and jailed. Women's visible contributions during the First World War further strengthened the cause. Congress approved the Nineteenth Amendment in 1919, and ratification was completed in August 1920, when Tennessee became the thirty-sixth state to approve the measure barring denial of the vote on account of sex.

title: Shrinking the Transistor
passage: In 1965, engineer Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors that could be fitted onto an integrated circuit was doubling at a regular interval, a trend later known as Moore's Law. For decades the observation held remarkably well: as manufacturers learned to etch ever-smaller components onto silicon wafers, chips became simultaneously faster, cheaper per transistor, and more energy efficient. A modern processor can contain billions of transistors, each acting as a microscopic switch that turns current on or off. Continued shrinking, however, has grown increasingly difficult. At extremely small scales, electrons can leak across barriers through a quantum effect called tunneling, and densely packed circuits generate heat that is hard to remove. Chipmakers have responded with new transistor geometries, three-dimensional stacking, and specialized processors tailored to particular tasks rather than relying on raw miniaturization alone. Whether such strategies can sustain historical rates of improvement remains an open question, but the era of easy gains from simple shrinking appears to be ending.

title: Light Through Glass Fibers
passage: Modern telecommunications depend heavily on optical fibers, hair-thin strands of extremely pure glass that carry information as pulses of light. Each fiber consists of a central core surrounded by a layer called cladding, which has a slightly lower refractive index than the core. Because of this difference, light striking the boundary at a shallow angle is reflected back inward, a phenomenon known as total internal reflection, and the signal can travel great distances while remaining trapped within the core. Compared with copper wire, fiber carries far more data and is immune to electromagnetic interference. Light does weaken gradually as it is absorbed and scattered, so long routes include amplifiers or repeaters that periodically restore signal strength. Networks of undersea fiber-optic cables link the continents and carry the overwhelming majority of intercontinental internet traffic. Because a single strand can carry many channels of light at different wavelengths simultaneously, engineers can often expand a cable's capacity simply by upgrading the equipment at its ends rather than laying new fiber.

title: Inside Lithium-Ion Batteries
passage: Lithium-ion batteries power devices from phones to electric vehicles because they store substantial energy in a small, lightweight package. During discharge, lithium ions travel through a liquid electrolyte from the negative electrode, typically graphite, to the positive electrode, while electrons flow through the external circuit and do useful work. Charging reverses the process, driving the ions back so the cell can be used again. First commercialized in 1991, the technology earned its pioneers the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Despite their advantages, lithium-ion cells require careful management. Overcharging, physical damage, or manufacturing defects can trigger thermal runaway, a self-accelerating reaction in which rising temperature releases energy that raises the temperature further, sometimes ending in fire. Battery packs therefore include electronic systems that continuously monitor voltage and temperature. Researchers continue to pursue improvements, including solid electrolytes intended to replace today's flammable liquid ones, in hopes of producing batteries that are both safer and more energy dense.

title: Why Concrete Needs Steel
passage: Concrete is among the most widely used construction materials on Earth, prized for its durability and its strength under compression. Unreinforced concrete, however, is weak in tension: a plain concrete beam that bends under load will crack on the side being stretched. Builders solve this problem by embedding steel bars, known as rebar, within the concrete before it hardens. The steel carries tensile forces while the surrounding concrete resists compression, allowing the composite to support loads neither material could bear alone. The partnership works partly because steel and concrete expand at nearly the same rate when heated, so ordinary temperature changes do not tear the two apart. Concrete also provides a highly alkaline environment that inhibits rusting of the embedded steel. That protection is not absolute; road salts and seawater can carry chloride ions into the concrete, corroding the rebar and causing the surface to crack and flake away. Engineers therefore specify thicker concrete cover, corrosion-resistant coatings, or other defenses for structures in harsh environments.

title: Machines That Dig Tunnels
passage: Beneath many of the world's cities, subway and utility tunnels are excavated not by crews with explosives but by tunnel boring machines, factory-like cylinders that can stretch longer than a football field. At the front, a rotating cutterhead studded with hardened steel discs grinds away rock and soil, while conveyors carry the excavated material back through the machine to waiting cars. Hydraulic jacks push the cutterhead forward, bracing against the concrete rings the machine itself installs: as it advances, it lifts curved precast segments into place behind it, so the machine leaves a finished, lined tunnel in its wake. Because all of this happens underground, boring machines disturb the surface far less than older cut-and-cover methods, in which streets were dug open and later rebuilt, a decisive advantage in dense urban areas. The machines are expensive to build and slow to assemble, so they make the most economic sense on long tunnels, such as the rail tunnel beneath the English Channel, much of which was carved by fleets of boring machines.

title: Controlling Nuclear Fission
passage: A nuclear power plant generates electricity from the energy released when heavy atoms split. In the most common reactor designs, a uranium-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes unstable and divides, releasing heat along with additional neutrons that can split further nuclei. Left unmanaged, this chain reaction would accelerate, so reactors are engineered to hold it steady. Control rods containing neutron-absorbing materials such as boron can be inserted into the core to slow the reaction or withdrawn to speed it up. Ordinary water often serves double duty, carrying heat away from the fuel while also slowing neutrons to speeds at which they are more likely to cause fission. The heat ultimately boils water into steam that spins turbine generators, much as in a coal-fired plant. Nuclear stations emit no carbon dioxide during operation and extract enormous energy from little fuel, yet they remain controversial because of high construction costs and the challenge of isolating radioactive waste for very long periods.
